questions.q: Which meningeal layer forms the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli?
questions.explain: The inner meningeal layer of the dura mater folds inward to form dural septa including the falx cerebri, tentorium cerebelli, falx cerebelli, and diaphragma sellae.

open.q: Name the tough outermost meningeal layer whose meningeal sheet folds inward to form the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli.

questions.q: A 28-year-old motorcyclist suffers a linear fracture of the temporal bone at the pterion, followed by a brief lucid interval and rapid neurological deterioration. Rupture of which vessel causes this classic epidural hematoma?
questions.explain: The anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery courses directly beneath the thin bone of the pterion; trauma here strips the periosteal dura from the skull, producing an arterial epidural hematoma.

open.q: Which artery lies directly deep to the pterion and is classically torn in temporal bone fractures to produce an epidural hematoma?
accept: anterior branch of middle meningeal artery

questions.q: An acute subdural hematoma most commonly results from tearing of which blood vessels?
options: Bridging veins entering dural sinuses, especially the superior sagittal sinus
questions.explain: Acceleration-deceleration trauma shears the thin-walled cerebral bridging veins as they traverse the subdural space to empty into the dural venous sinuses, particularly the superior sagittal sinus.

open.q: Rupture of which venous structures traversing the subdural space into the dural venous sinuses is the most frequent cause of a subdural hematoma?

questions.q: Which cranial nerve runs freely through the lumen of the cavernous sinus alongside the internal carotid artery rather than within its lateral dural wall?
questions.explain: The abducens nerve (CN VI) courses directly through the cavernous sinus inferolateral to the internal carotid artery, making it the first cranial nerve affected in cavernous sinus thrombosis or internal carotid aneurysms.

open.q: Which cranial nerve passes directly through the interior of the cavernous sinus adjacent to the internal carotid artery rather than in its lateral wall?

questions.q: The straight sinus is formed at the junction of the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli by the union of the inferior sagittal sinus and which vein?
questions.explain: The great cerebral vein (of Galen) unites with the inferior sagittal sinus at the anterior apex of the tentorium cerebelli to form the straight sinus, which drains posteriorly into the confluence of sinuses.

open.q: Which deep cerebral vein joins the inferior sagittal sinus to form the straight sinus?

questions.q: Through which paired openings does cerebrospinal fluid pass from the lateral ventricles into the third ventricle?
questions.explain: CSF flows from each lateral ventricle into the midline third ventricle via the right and left interventricular foramina (of Monro), located just posterior to the columns of the fornix.

open.q: Name the paired openings connecting the lateral ventricles to the third ventricle.

questions.q: Stenosis of the cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius) results in enlargement of which ventricles?
questions.explain: Because the cerebral aqueduct connects the third ventricle to the fourth ventricle through the midbrain, aqueductal stenosis causes non-communicating hydrocephalus with dilation of the lateral and third ventricles while sparing the fourth ventricle.

open.q: Which ventricles dilate proximal to an obstruction of the cerebral aqueduct?

questions.q: Where is cerebrospinal fluid primarily absorbed back into the venous circulation?
options: Arachnoid villi and granulations, mainly into the superior sagittal sinus
questions.explain: Arachnoid villi and granulations herniate through the meningeal dura into the dural venous sinuses (chiefly the superior sagittal sinus), acting as one-way pressure-dependent valves returning CSF to venous blood.

open.q: Name the specialized projections of the arachnoid mater into the superior sagittal sinus responsible for reabsorbing cerebrospinal fluid.

questions.q: In a normal adult, at which vertebral level does the conus medullaris of the spinal cord terminate?
questions.explain: Due to differential growth of the vertebral column and spinal cord, the adult conus medullaris ends at the L1-L2 vertebral level (whereas in a newborn it lies around L3), allowing safe lumbar puncture at L3-L4 or L4-L5.

open.q: At which lumbar vertebral level does the spinal cord typically terminate as the conus medullaris in an adult?

questions.q: Which pial specialization anchors the conus medullaris inferiorly to the posterior surface of the coccyx?
questions.explain: The filum terminale is a delicate fibrous strand of pia mater extending from the apex of the conus medullaris through the dural sac (at S2) to attach to the dorsum of the coccyx.

open.q: Name the slender fibrous filament of pia mater that extends from the tip of the conus medullaris to anchor onto the coccyx.

questions.q: From which meningeal layer are the paired denticulate ligaments derived to suspend the spinal cord laterally?
questions.explain: The 21 pairs of tooth-like denticulate ligaments are lateral extensions of the spinal pia mater that attach to the arachnoid and dura mater midway between the dorsal and ventral nerve roots.

open.q: Which meningeal layer gives rise to the denticulate ligaments that stabilize the spinal cord laterally within the dural sac?

questions.q: Where do second-order neurons of the dorsal column-medial lemniscus (DCML) pathway decussate?
options: Caudal medulla as internal arcuate fibers
Anterior white commissure of the spinal cord
Midbrain at the superior cerebellar peduncle
questions.explain: First-order DCML axons ascend ipsilaterally in the fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus to synapse in the nucleus gracilis and cuneatus; second-order axons then cross the midline in the lower medulla as internal arcuate fibers to form the contralateral medial lemniscus.

open.q: Where in the central nervous system do second-order axons of the dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway decussate?

questions.q: Second-order neurons of the lateral spinothalamic tract decussate in which spinal cord structure before ascending contralaterally?
questions.explain: First-order pain and temperature fibers ascend 1 to 2 segments in Lissauer tract, synapse in the substantia gelatinosa, and second-order axons cross obliquely via the anterior white commissure to enter the contralateral lateral spinothalamic tract.

open.q: Through which commissure of the spinal cord do second-order axons of the spinothalamic tract cross to the opposite side?

questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with bilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation across his shoulders and upper limbs ('cape-like' distribution) while light touch and vibration remain intact. Expansion of the central canal (syringomyelia) damages which structure?
questions.explain: A cervical syrinx expands outward from the central canal and selectively interrupts decussating spinothalamic fibers in the anterior white commissure, causing dissociated bilateral pain and temperature loss at the affected dermatomes.

open.q: Which spinal cord pathway structure is damaged by an expanding cervical syrinx to cause bilateral cape-like loss of pain and temperature?

questions.q: A patient sustains a knife wound causing right-sided hemisection of the spinal cord at T8 (Brown-Sequard syndrome). Which deficit is present on the LEFT side below the lesion?
options: Contralateral pain and temperature loss beginning 1–2 segments below T8
Left-foot loss of vibration and proprioception
questions.explain: Because spinothalamic fibers cross in the spinal cord 1 to 2 segments above entry, a right T8 hemisection causes contralateral (left) loss of pain and temperature below ~T9-T10, alongside ipsilateral (right) UMN paralysis and DCML loss.

open.q: In right-sided spinal cord hemisection (Brown-Sequard syndrome), which sensory modalities are lost on the contralateral (left) side below the lesion?

questions.q: Where do approximately 85% to 90% of corticospinal tract fibers cross the midline to form the lateral corticospinal tract?
questions.explain: At the spinomedullary junction in the caudal medulla, roughly 85-90% of pyramidal fibers decussate to descend in the contralateral lateral funiculus as the lateral corticospinal tract.

open.q: At which brainstem level do the majority of corticospinal fibers cross the midline in the pyramidal decussation?

questions.q: Which cranial nerve emerges from the dorsal aspect of the brainstem just inferior to the inferior colliculus?
questions.explain: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is the only cranial nerve to emerge from the dorsal surface of the brainstem and decussates completely in the superior medullary velum before exiting.

open.q: Name the only cranial nerve that exits from the dorsal surface of the brainstem.

questions.q: The facial colliculus on the dorsal floor of the fourth ventricle in the pons is formed by fibers of the facial nerve looping over which nucleus?
questions.explain: Motor axons from the facial motor nucleus loop dorsally around the abducens nucleus (forming the internal genu of CN VII) before exiting the pontomedullary junction, raising the facial colliculus.

open.q: Fibers of the facial nerve loop around which cranial nerve nucleus to create the elevation known as the facial colliculus?

questions.q: Which cranial nerve emerges from the preolivary sulcus between the pyramid and the olive of the medulla oblongata?
questions.explain: The rootlets of the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) emerge anteriorly in the preolivary sulcus between the pyramid and the olive, whereas CN IX, X, and cranial XI emerge from the postolivary (retro-olivary) sulcus.

open.q: Which cranial nerve exits the medulla oblongata anteriorly through the preolivary sulcus between the pyramid and the olive?

questions.q: Occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) or vertebral artery causes lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome. Which finding is uniquely characteristic of this syndrome due to nucleus ambiguus damage?
options: Dysphagia, hoarseness, and loss of the gag reflex
questions.explain: Lateral medullary syndrome damages the nucleus ambiguus (causing dysphagia, dysarthria/hoarseness, and absent gag reflex), spinal trigeminal nucleus, spinothalamic tract, vestibular nuclei, and descending sympathetic fibers (Horner syndrome), while sparing the medial corticospinal and hypoglossal structures.

open.q: Damage to which motor nucleus in lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome produces dysphagia, hoarseness, and loss of the gag reflex?

questions.q: Which visceral sensory nucleus in the dorsal medulla receives taste afferents from CN VII, IX, and X as well as baroreceptor and chemoreceptor afferents from the carotid sinus and aortic arch?
options: Dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus
questions.explain: The rostral gustatory part of the nucleus tractus solitarius processes taste (CN VII, IX, X), while its caudal cardiorespiratory part receives general visceral afferents (CN IX, X) from baroreceptors, chemoreceptors, and thoracic/abdominal viscera.

open.q: Name the medullary nucleus that receives both gustatory afferents and visceral baroreceptor/chemoreceptor input via CN VII, IX, and X.

questions.q: Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers responsible for pupillary constriction and lens accommodation originate from which midbrain nucleus?
questions.explain: The Edinger-Westphal nucleus sits dorsal to the somatic oculomotor nucleus in the rostral midbrain and sends preganglionic parasympathetic axons via CN III to synapse in the ciliary ganglion.

open.q: From which midbrain parasympathetic nucleus do preganglionic fibers travel with the oculomotor nerve to the ciliary ganglion?

questions.q: Through which cerebellar peduncle do climbing fibers from the contralateral inferior olivary nucleus enter the cerebellum?
questions.explain: Olivocerebellar climbing fibers cross the midline and enter the cerebellum exclusively via the inferior cerebellar peduncle, along with dorsal spinocerebellar and vestibulocerebellar afferents.

open.q: Through which cerebellar peduncle do olivocerebellar climbing fibers and dorsal spinocerebellar axons enter the cerebellum?

questions.q: Which cerebellar peduncle carries the major efferent output from the dentate, emboliform, and globose nuclei to the contralateral red nucleus and thalamus?
questions.explain: The superior cerebellar peduncle is the primary output pathway of the cerebellum; its fibers decussate in the caudal midbrain to reach the contralateral red nucleus and ventral lateral (VL) nucleus of the thalamus.

open.q: Which cerebellar peduncle serves as the main efferent outflow tract from the deep cerebellar nuclei to the contralateral thalamus and red nucleus?

questions.q: Which neurons provide the sole efferent output of the cerebellar cortex, projecting inhibitory GABAergic axons to the deep cerebellar nuclei?
questions.explain: Purkinje cells are large flask-shaped neurons arranged in a single layer whose axons form the only efferent output from the cerebellar cortex, exerting GABAergic inhibition on the deep cerebellar and vestibular nuclei.

open.q: Name the sole output neurons of the cerebellar cortex that send inhibitory GABAergic projections to the deep cerebellar nuclei.

questions.q: A lesion of the right cerebellar hemisphere causes limb ataxia on which side of the body?
questions.explain: Cerebellar hemisphere lesions produce ipsilateral motor deficits (dysmetria, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia) because cerebellar output crosses twice: once in the superior cerebellar peduncle decussation and back again via the corticospinal pyramidal decussation.

open.q: Does a unilateral lesion of the cerebellar hemisphere cause ipsilateral or contralateral limb ataxia?

questions.q: Which thalamic relay nucleus receives somatosensory input from the medial lemniscus and spinothalamic tracts and projects to the primary somatosensory cortex?
questions.explain: The VPL nucleus relays body somatosensory information (from the medial lemniscus and spinothalamic tracts) to the postcentral gyrus, whereas the VPM nucleus relays facial somatosensation and taste from the trigeminal and solitary pathways.

open.q: Which thalamic nucleus relays somatic sensory signals from the trunk and limbs to the primary somatosensory cortex?

questions.q: Which thalamic nucleus serves as the primary relay station for visual information from the optic tract to the primary visual cortex?
questions.explain: Axons of retinal ganglion cells travel in the optic tract to synapse in the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus, which projects via the optic radiation to area 17 in the occipital lobe.

open.q: Name the thalamic relay nucleus that receives retinal fibers from the optic tract and projects to the primary visual cortex.

questions.q: Which two hypothalamic nuclei synthesize oxytocin and antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) for transport down the hypothalamohypophyseal tract to the neurohypophysis?
questions.explain: Magnocellular neurons in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus synthesize ADH (predominantly supraoptic) and oxytocin (predominantly paraventricular) and transport them to the posterior pituitary.

open.q: Name the two hypothalamic nuclei that synthesize antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) and oxytocin.

questions.q: Which hypothalamic nucleus acts as the master circadian pacemaker and receives direct retinohypothalamic input?
questions.explain: The suprachiasmatic nucleus lies immediately superior to the optic chiasm and regulates circadian rhythms in response to light signals carried by the retinohypothalamic tract.

open.q: Which hypothalamic nucleus situated directly above the optic chiasm regulates circadian rhythms?

questions.q: Which structures together constitute the corpus striatum (and specifically the lentiform nucleus)?
options: Putamen plus globus pallidus form lentiform nucleus; adding caudate forms corpus striatum
Thalamus plus subthalamic nucleus form lentiform nucleus
Substantia nigra plus red nucleus form corpus striatum
Amygdala plus hippocampus form lentiform nucleus
questions.explain: The lentiform (lenticular) nucleus consists of the lateral putamen and medial globus pallidus; together with the caudate nucleus, it forms the corpus striatum.

open.q: Which two basal ganglia structures combine to form the lens-shaped lentiform nucleus?

questions.q: Degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in which midbrain structure projecting to the striatum causes Parkinson disease?
questions.explain: Loss of pigmented dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta depletes nigrostriatal dopamine, reducing direct pathway facilitation and increasing indirect pathway inhibition of movement.

open.q: Loss of dopaminergic neurons in which subdivision of the substantia nigra underlies Parkinson disease?

questions.q: An elderly hypertensive patient suddenly develops violent, involuntary flinging movements of his left arm and leg (left hemiballismus). A small lacunar infarct is most likely located in which contralateral structure?
questions.explain: Hemiballismus is caused by a lesion (typically a lacunar stroke) in the contralateral subthalamic nucleus, removing excitatory drive to the globus pallidus internus and disinhibiting thalamocortical motor pathways.

open.q: A vascular lesion in which contralateral diencephalic nucleus classically produces hemiballismus?

questions.q: Which motor tract descends through the genu of the internal capsule?
questions.explain: The genu of the internal capsule transmits corticobulbar fibers supplying cranial nerve motor nuclei, whereas corticospinal fibers descend through the anterior two-thirds of the posterior limb.

open.q: Which descending motor pathway passes through the genu of the internal capsule?

questions.q: Which deep perforating arteries, arising primarily from the M1 segment of the middle cerebral artery, supply the posterior limb of the internal capsule and lentiform nucleus?
questions.explain: The lateral lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery pierce the anterior perforated substance to supply the lentiform nucleus, caudate, and posterior limb of the internal capsule—commonly rupturing in hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage.

open.q: Name the perforating branches of the middle cerebral artery that supply the internal capsule and basal ganglia and frequently rupture in hypertension.

questions.q: Where is the primary motor cortex (Brodmann area 4) located?
options: Precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe
Postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe
Cuneus and lingual gyrus of the occipital lobe
questions.explain: The primary motor cortex (Brodmann area 4) occupies the precentral gyrus immediately anterior to the central sulcus and the anterior part of the paracentral lobule.

open.q: In which gyrus of the frontal lobe is the primary motor cortex (Brodmann area 4) situated?

questions.q: Which cortical region on the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere contains the motor and sensory representation of the contralateral lower limb and perineum?
questions.explain: The paracentral lobule surrounds the medial continuation of the central sulcus and represents the lower extremity, foot, and perineum/bladder control, supplied by the anterior cerebral artery.

open.q: Name the medial cortical lobule surrounding the upper end of the central sulcus that controls the contralateral lower limb and perineum.

questions.q: Broca expressive speech area (Brodmann areas 44 and 45) is located in which gyrus of the dominant frontal lobe?
options: Inferior frontal gyrus (pars opercularis and triangularis)
questions.explain: Broca area lies in the pars opercularis and pars triangularis of the inferior frontal gyrus in the dominant (usually left) hemisphere and coordinates motor speech production.

open.q: In which gyrus of the dominant frontal lobe is Broca motor speech area (areas 44 and 45) located?

questions.q: Which major white matter association bundle connects Wernicke receptive language area in the temporal lobe with Broca area in the frontal lobe?
options: Arcuate fasciculus, within the superior longitudinal fasciculus
questions.explain: The arcuate fasciculus arches around the posterior end of the lateral sulcus to link Wernicke area (area 22) with Broca area (areas 44/45); damage produces conduction aphasia with impaired repetition.

open.q: Name the curved white matter association tract that links Wernicke area to Broca area.

questions.q: The primary visual cortex (Brodmann area 17, striate cortex) is located along the upper and lower banks of which sulcus?
questions.explain: The primary visual cortex lines the upper (cuneus) and lower (lingual gyrus) lips of the calcarine sulcus on the medial aspect of the occipital lobe.

open.q: Along the banks of which occipital sulcus is the primary visual cortex (Brodmann area 17) located?

questions.q: Which C-shaped white matter bundle carries the major efferent output from the hippocampus to the mammillary bodies of the hypothalamus?
questions.explain: The fornix arises from the alveus and fimbria of the hippocampus, arches beneath the corpus callosum, and divides into columns that terminate predominantly in the mammillary bodies.

open.q: Name the arched white matter fiber tract that projects from the hippocampus to the mammillary bodies.

questions.q: In the Papez circuit of memory and emotion, the mammillothalamic tract projects from the mammillary bodies to which thalamic nucleus?
questions.explain: The Papez circuit runs: hippocampus -> fornix -> mammillary bodies -> mammillothalamic tract -> anterior thalamic nucleus -> cingulate gyrus -> parahippocampal gyrus -> hippocampus.

open.q: To which thalamic nucleus does the mammillothalamic tract project within the Papez circuit?

questions.sub: Cerebral Blood Supply and Circle of Willis
questions.q: Which artery connects the right and left anterior cerebral arteries across the longitudinal fissure to complete the anterior portion of the circle of Willis?
questions.explain: The short anterior communicating artery links the two anterior cerebral arteries just anterior to the optic chiasm and is the single most common site of saccular (berry) aneurysms.

open.q: Which short unpaired artery bridges the right and left anterior cerebral arteries in the circle of Willis?

questions.sub: Cerebral Blood Supply and Circle of Willis
questions.q: A 46-year-old woman presents with sudden ptosis, a 'down and out' right eye, and a fixed dilated right pupil due to compression of the oculomotor nerve. A berry aneurysm at the junction of the internal carotid artery and which artery is most likely responsible?
questions.explain: The oculomotor nerve (CN III) passes directly alongside the posterior communicating artery between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries, making CN III palsy a classic sign of a posterior communicating artery aneurysm.

open.q: A berry aneurysm of which artery in the circle of Willis classically compresses the adjacent oculomotor nerve (CN III)?

questions.sub: Cerebral Blood Supply and Circle of Willis
questions.q: A 64-year-old man develops acute weakness and sensory loss predominantly affecting his right lower limb and foot, accompanied by urinary incontinence, while his right face and arm are spared. Which artery is occluded?
questions.explain: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes including the paracentral lobule (contralateral lower limb and perineal/bladder representation).

open.q: Occlusion of which cerebral artery produces contralateral lower-limb motor and sensory deficits with urinary incontinence?

questions.sub: Cerebral Blood Supply and Circle of Willis
questions.q: In a posterior cerebral artery stroke causing contralateral homonymous hemianopia, why is central macular vision often preserved ('macular sparing')?
options: MCA collateral flow may preserve the macular occipital pole
questions.explain: The posterior tip of the occipital pole (where the macula is represented) lies at an anastomotic watershed receiving collateral blood flow from terminal branches of the middle cerebral artery, frequently sparing macular vision in PCA occlusion.

open.q: Which cerebral artery provides collateral blood supply to the occipital pole, explaining macular sparing in posterior cerebral artery strokes?

questions.sub: Cerebral Blood Supply and Circle of Willis
questions.q: Which artery supplies the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord and is formed by the union of branches from the two vertebral arteries?
questions.explain: The single anterior spinal artery descends in the anterior median fissure and supplies the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord, including the lateral corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts.

open.q: Which single longitudinal artery runs in the anterior median fissure to supply the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord?

questions.sub: Cerebral Blood Supply and Circle of Willis
questions.q: The great anterior radicular artery (artery of Adamkiewicz) reinforces the anterior spinal artery in the thoracolumbar region and most commonly arises on which side between T8 and L2?
questions.explain: In roughly 75-80% of individuals, the artery of Adamkiewicz arises on the left side from a lower posterior intercostal or upper lumbar branch of the aorta (T8-L2) to supply the lumbosacral enlargement of the spinal cord.

open.q: On which side of the body does the great anterior radicular artery (artery of Adamkiewicz) most commonly arise?

questions.q: A patient with a large right temporal lobe mass develops a dilated, unreactive right pupil followed by left-sided hemiparesis and coma. Which type of brain herniation compresses the ipsilateral oculomotor nerve and cerebral peduncle against the tentorial notch?
questions.explain: In uncal herniation, the medial temporal uncus shifts medially over the free edge of the tentorium cerebelli, compressing the ipsilateral CN III (causing a blown pupil) and the adjacent cerebral peduncle (causing contralateral hemiparesis).

open.q: Name the type of brain herniation in which the medial temporal lobe herniates across the tentorial notch, compressing the ipsilateral oculomotor nerve.

questions.q: Performing a lumbar puncture in a patient with markedly elevated supratentorial intracranial pressure risks precipitating which immediately life-threatening herniation through the foramen magnum?
questions.explain: Rapid withdrawal of lumbar CSF creates a downward pressure gradient that forces the cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum, compressing the medullary cardiorespiratory centers and causing sudden respiratory and cardiac arrest.

open.q: Which cerebellar structures herniate downward through the foramen magnum to compress the medulla oblongata when intracranial pressure drops abruptly below?

questions.q: An epidural catheter is placed for regional anaesthesia. In which space should its tip lie, and what normally occupies that space?
options: Epidural space containing fat and the internal vertebral venous plexus
questions.explain: The spinal epidural space lies between the vertebral canal periosteum/ligaments and the spinal dura mater. It contains loose connective tissue, fat and the internal vertebral venous plexus; epidural anaesthetic is delivered outside the dural sac.

open.q: What are two important contents of the spinal epidural space?
accept: fat and the internal vertebral venous plexus
epidural fat and internal vertebral venous plexus
loose connective tissue and internal vertebral venous plexus

questions.q: During a lumbar puncture in an adult, the needle enters the lumbar cistern below the termination of the spinal cord. Which collection of nerve roots is present in this region?
questions.explain: The conus medullaris usually ends around the L1-L2 vertebral level in adults. Below it, lumbar and sacral nerve roots descend through the lumbar cistern as the cauda equina, suspended in cerebrospinal fluid; this anatomy permits a correctly performed lower lumbar puncture.

open.q: What is the name of the bundle of descending lumbar and sacral nerve roots in the lumbar cistern?

questions.q: A small infarct selectively damages the posterior spinal arteries. Which region of the spinal cord is most likely to become ischaemic?
options: Anterior horns and most of the anterolateral cord
Posterior one-third of the spinal cord
questions.explain: The paired posterior spinal arteries supply approximately the posterior one-third of the spinal cord, including much of the dorsal columns and posterior horns. The anterior spinal artery supplies most of the anterior two-thirds.

open.q: Which portion of the spinal cord is supplied predominantly by the paired posterior spinal arteries?
accept: posterior third of the spinal cord
dorsal one-third of the spinal cord

questions.q: A sample of cerebrospinal fluid is obtained from the lumbar cistern. Between which meningeal layers is this fluid normally found?
options: Between dura mater and arachnoid mater
Between arachnoid mater and pia mater
Between pia mater and spinal cord tissue
questions.explain: Cerebrospinal fluid occupies the subarachnoid space between the arachnoid mater and pia mater. In the lumbar cistern, this space extends below the conus medullaris and surrounds the cauda equina.

open.q: Between which two meningeal layers is cerebrospinal fluid found in the lumbar cistern?

questions.q: Which pair of cranial nerves is not attached to the brainstem?
questions.explain: The olfactory and optic nerves attach to the forebrain. The other ten pairs are attached to the brainstem.

open.q: Which two cranial nerves are not attached to the brainstem?

questions.q: Which cranial nerve has a root that ascends through the foramen magnum before leaving the skull through the jugular foramen?
questions.explain: The spinal root of the accessory nerve arises from the upper cervical cord, ascends through the foramen magnum and then exits through the jugular foramen.

open.q: Which cranial nerve has a spinal root that ascends through the foramen magnum before leaving through the jugular foramen?

questions.q: Which cranial nerve emerges from the dorsal surface of the brainstem?
questions.explain: The trochlear nerve is the only cranial nerve to emerge dorsally, just below the inferior colliculus.

open.q: Which cranial nerve emerges from the dorsal surface of the brainstem?

questions.q: Which cranial nerve leaves the skull through the hypoglossal canal?
questions.explain: The hypoglossal nerve exits through the hypoglossal canal in the occipital bone. CN IX, X and XI leave through the jugular foramen.

open.q: Which cranial nerve leaves the skull through the hypoglossal canal?

questions.q: Through which structure do the olfactory nerve fibres pass from the nasal cavity into the anterior cranial fossa?
questions.explain: Olfactory nerve fibres pass through the foramina of the cribriform plate to reach the olfactory bulb.

open.q: Through which structure do olfactory nerve fibres pass from the nasal cavity into the anterior cranial fossa?

questions.q: What is the most common cause of anosmia after head trauma?
options: Shearing of olfactory fibres at the cribriform plate
Compression of the optic chiasm by a haematoma
Stretching of the oculomotor nerve in the cavernous sinus
Tearing of the facial nerve in the temporal bone
questions.explain: The brain moves relative to the fixed skull and the delicate olfactory fibres are sheared as they cross the cribriform plate. CSF rhinorrhoea may also occur.

open.q: What is the most common mechanism of anosmia after head trauma?
accept: shearing of olfactory fibres at the cribriform plate

questions.q: Which special sense reaches the cerebral cortex without a relay in the thalamus?
questions.explain: Olfactory pathways pass directly to the olfactory cortex of the temporal lobe. All other sensory pathways relay in the thalamus.

open.q: Which special sense reaches the cerebral cortex without a relay in the thalamus?

questions.q: Olfactory hallucinations, such as smelling a strange odour before a seizure, usually arise from irritation of which region?
questions.explain: The uncus is part of the primary olfactory cortex, and irritative lesions there cause uncinate fits.

open.q: Olfactory hallucinations before a seizure usually arise from irritation of which part of the temporal lobe?
accept: olfactory cortex of the temporal lobe

questions.q: Because the optic nerve is a CNS tract, which coverings does it have?
options: Periosteum of the optic canal only
questions.explain: The optic nerve is an outgrowth of the diencephalon, so it is ensheathed by dura, arachnoid and pia. Raised intracranial pressure is therefore transmitted to the optic disc and causes papilloedema.

open.q: What coverings does the optic nerve have, given that it is an extension of the brain?

questions.q: Optic neuritis is most commonly associated with which disease?
questions.explain: Optic neuritis is demyelination of the optic nerve and is a common first presentation of multiple sclerosis.

open.q: Optic neuritis is most commonly associated with which demyelinating disease?

questions.q: A man with headaches and a pituitary adenoma loses peripheral vision on both sides. Which visual field defect does he have?
questions.explain: The tumour compresses the optic chiasm and damages the crossing nasal retinal fibres, so the temporal visual fields are lost.

open.q: A man with a pituitary adenoma loses peripheral vision on both sides. What visual field defect does he have?

questions.q: A lesion of the right optic tract produces which visual field defect?
questions.explain: The right optic tract carries fibres from the right half of each retina, which see the left visual field. A lesion therefore causes loss of the left half of the field in both eyes.

open.q: A lesion of the right optic tract produces which visual field defect?

questions.q: In a complete oculomotor nerve palsy, where does the eye rest?
questions.explain: The unopposed lateral rectus (CN VI) abducts the eye and the superior oblique (CN IV) depresses it, so the eye looks down and out.

open.q: In a complete oculomotor nerve palsy, in which direction does the eye rest?

questions.q: Ptosis in an oculomotor nerve palsy is due to paralysis of which muscle?
questions.explain: Levator palpebrae superioris is supplied by CN III. Orbicularis oculi and the other options are supplied by the facial nerve.

open.q: Ptosis in an oculomotor nerve palsy is due to paralysis of which muscle?

questions.q: The parasympathetic fibres of the oculomotor nerve arise from which nucleus?
questions.explain: The Edinger-Westphal nucleus gives preganglionic fibres to the ciliary ganglion for pupillary constriction and accommodation.

open.q: From which nucleus do the parasympathetic fibres of the oculomotor nerve arise?

questions.q: In which parasympathetic ganglion do the oculomotor preganglionic fibres synapse?
questions.explain: Postganglionic fibres from the ciliary ganglion supply sphincter pupillae and ciliaris via the short ciliary nerves.

open.q: In which parasympathetic ganglion do the oculomotor preganglionic fibres synapse?

questions.q: A patient with an expanding extradural haematoma develops a dilated, non-reactive pupil on the same side. Which nerve is being compressed?
questions.explain: The parasympathetic fibres lie on the outside of the oculomotor nerve, so uncal herniation compresses them early. The pupil dilates and stops reacting to light.

open.q: A patient with an expanding extradural haematoma develops a dilated, non-reactive pupil on the same side. Which nerve is being compressed?

questions.q: As it leaves the midbrain, the oculomotor nerve passes between which two arteries?
questions.explain: Aneurysms of these arteries can compress the oculomotor nerve and cause a CN III palsy.

open.q: As it leaves the midbrain, the oculomotor nerve passes between which two arteries?
accept: posterior cerebral artery and superior cerebellar artery
superior cerebellar and posterior cerebral arteries

questions.q: Which extraocular muscle is supplied by the trochlear nerve?
questions.explain: The trochlear nerve supplies only the superior oblique. A memory aid is LR6 SO4 AO3.

open.q: Which extraocular muscle is supplied by the trochlear nerve?

questions.q: Which cranial nerve is the most slender and has the longest intracranial course?
questions.explain: The trochlear nerve emerges dorsally, winds around the cerebral peduncle and runs a long way before reaching the orbit.

open.q: Which cranial nerve is the most slender and has the longest intracranial course?

questions.q: In trochlear nerve palsy, diplopia is worst during which activity?
questions.explain: The superior oblique depresses the adducted eye. Loss of this action causes vertical diplopia when looking down and inward.

open.q: In trochlear nerve palsy, diplopia is worst during which everyday activity?

questions.q: The motor root of the trigeminal nerve supplies which group of muscles?
questions.explain: The mandibular nerve carries the motor fibres to the muscles of mastication, tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini, mylohyoid and anterior belly of digastric.

open.q: The motor root of the trigeminal nerve supplies which group of muscles?

questions.q: Through which foramen does the maxillary nerve (V2) leave the cranial cavity?
questions.explain: V2 passes through the foramen rotundum into the pterygopalatine fossa.

open.q: Through which foramen does the maxillary nerve leave the cranial cavity?

questions.q: Through which foramen does the mandibular nerve (V3) leave the cranial cavity?
questions.explain: V3 leaves through the foramen ovale into the infratemporal fossa. The middle meningeal artery passes through the foramen spinosum.

open.q: Through which foramen does the mandibular nerve leave the cranial cavity?

questions.q: Through which opening does the ophthalmic nerve (V1) enter the orbit?
questions.explain: V1 enters the orbit via the superior orbital fissure, together with CN III, IV and VI.

open.q: Through which opening does the ophthalmic nerve enter the orbit?

questions.q: Which nerve carries the afferent limb of the corneal reflex?
questions.explain: The nasociliary branch of V1 carries the sensation from the cornea. The efferent limb is the facial nerve to orbicularis oculi.

open.q: Which nerve carries the afferent limb of the corneal reflex?

questions.q: How does trigeminal neuralgia typically present?
options: Loss of taste on the tongue
questions.explain: It causes paroxysms of lancinating pain in one or more divisions, usually V2 or V3, often triggered by touch, chewing or cold.

open.q: How does trigeminal neuralgia typically present?
accept: severe lancinating pain in the face

questions.q: An inferior alveolar nerve block anaesthetises the lower teeth. Which division of the trigeminal nerve gives rise to this nerve?
questions.explain: The inferior alveolar nerve is a branch of the mandibular division (V3) and enters the mandibular foramen.

open.q: An inferior alveolar nerve block anaesthetises the lower teeth. Which division of the trigeminal nerve gives rise to this nerve?

questions.q: A patient's jaw deviates to the right when she opens her mouth. Which nerve is damaged?
questions.explain: The lateral pterygoid on the damaged side cannot protrude the jaw, so the unopposed muscle on the normal side pushes the jaw toward the weak side.

open.q: A patient's jaw deviates to the right when she opens her mouth. Which nerve is damaged?

questions.q: Which extraocular muscle is supplied by the abducent nerve?
questions.explain: The abducent nerve supplies only the lateral rectus, which abducts the eye.

open.q: Which extraocular muscle is supplied by the abducent nerve?

questions.q: In abducent nerve palsy, in which direction is the eye deviated at rest?
questions.explain: The unopposed medial rectus pulls the eye inward, causing a convergent squint and horizontal diplopia that is worse on looking toward the affected side.

open.q: In abducent nerve palsy, in which direction is the eye deviated at rest?

questions.q: Why is the abducent nerve often affected first when intracranial pressure rises?
options: It has a very large diameter
It is stretched over the petrous ridge
It runs through the foramen rotundum
questions.explain: Downward displacement of the brainstem stretches the nerve over the petrous ridge of the temporal bone. A CN VI palsy in raised pressure is a false localising sign.

open.q: Why is the abducent nerve often affected first when intracranial pressure rises?
accept: stretched over the petrous temporal bone
long course with stretching over the petrous ridge

questions.q: Through which foramen does the facial nerve leave the skull to reach the face?
questions.explain: The facial nerve runs through the facial canal and exits at the stylomastoid foramen, then enters the parotid gland.

open.q: Through which foramen does the facial nerve leave the skull to reach the face?

questions.q: Which nerve carries taste from the anterior two thirds of the tongue?
questions.explain: The chorda tympani, a branch of the facial nerve, joins the lingual nerve and carries taste from the anterior two thirds of the tongue.

open.q: Which nerve carries taste from the anterior two thirds of the tongue?
accept: chorda tympani branch of facial nerve
facial nerve via the chorda tympani

questions.q: Which branch of the facial nerve carries parasympathetic fibres to the lacrimal gland?
questions.explain: The greater petrosal nerve joins the deep petrosal nerve to form the nerve of the pterygoid canal and synapses in the pterygopalatine ganglion.

open.q: Which branch of the facial nerve carries parasympathetic fibres to the lacrimal gland?

questions.q: Hyperacusis in facial nerve palsy is due to paralysis of which muscle?
questions.explain: The nerve to stapedius normally dampens ossicular movement. Without it, sounds are abnormally loud.

open.q: Hyperacusis in facial nerve palsy is due to paralysis of which middle-ear muscle?

questions.q: A woman cannot close her left eye or wrinkle her left forehead, and her left mouth droops. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explain: Paralysis of the whole half of the face, including the forehead, indicates a lower motor neurone lesion of the facial nerve, as in Bell palsy. A hemisphere stroke would spare the forehead.

open.q: A woman cannot close her left eye or wrinkle her left forehead, and her left mouth droops. What is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.q: Why is the forehead spared in an upper motor neurone facial lesion?
options: Bilateral cortical input to upper facial neurones
Trigeminal innervation of the frontalis muscle
Oculomotor innervation of the frontalis muscle
Cervical branch innervation of the forehead
questions.explain: The facial nucleus neurones for the upper face receive input from both cerebral hemispheres, so a one-sided cortical lesion spares the forehead.

open.q: Why is the forehead spared in an upper motor neurone facial lesion?
accept: bilateral cortical innervation of the upper face
upper face has input from both hemispheres
bilateral corticobulbar supply to the forehead

questions.q: Which salivary glands receive parasympathetic secretomotor fibres from the facial nerve?
questions.explain: Fibres travel in the chorda tympani and lingual nerve to the submandibular ganglion. The parotid is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve.

open.q: Which salivary glands receive parasympathetic secretomotor fibres from the facial nerve?

questions.q: Through which opening does the vestibulocochlear nerve leave the posterior cranial fossa?
questions.explain: CN VII and CN VIII enter the internal acoustic meatus together. CN VIII then divides into cochlear and vestibular parts.

open.q: Through which opening does the vestibulocochlear nerve leave the posterior cranial fossa?

questions.q: At which site does an acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma) most commonly arise?
questions.explain: The tumour arises from Schwann cells of the vestibular division. It causes hearing loss, tinnitus and vertigo, and it may press on CN V and CN VII.

open.q: At which site does an acoustic neuroma most commonly arise?

questions.q: Which muscle is the only one supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve?
questions.explain: Stylopharyngeus is the only muscle supplied by CN IX. It elevates the pharynx during swallowing.

open.q: Which muscle is the only one supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve?

questions.q: In which ganglion do the glossopharyngeal preganglionic fibres to the parotid gland synapse?
questions.explain: Fibres run in the tympanic branch and the lesser petrosal nerve to the otic ganglion, and then to the parotid via the auriculotemporal nerve.

open.q: In which ganglion do the glossopharyngeal preganglionic fibres to the parotid gland synapse?

questions.q: Which cranial nerve carries the afferent limb of the gag reflex?
questions.explain: CN IX carries pharyngeal sensation, and the efferent limb is mainly the vagus nerve.

open.q: Which cranial nerve carries the afferent limb of the gag reflex?

questions.q: Which nerve carries information from the baroreceptors of the carotid sinus?
questions.explain: The carotid sinus nerve, a branch of CN IX, carries baroreceptor and carotid body chemoreceptor input to the brainstem.

open.q: Which cranial nerve carries information from the baroreceptors of the carotid sinus?

questions.q: Which nerve carries taste from the posterior third of the tongue?
questions.explain: CN IX supplies both general sensation and taste from the posterior third of the tongue.

open.q: Which nerve carries taste from the posterior third of the tongue?

questions.q: Which intrinsic laryngeal muscle is not supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve?
questions.explain: Cricothyroid is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve, a branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. All other intrinsic muscles are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

open.q: Which intrinsic laryngeal muscle is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve instead of the recurrent laryngeal nerve?

questions.q: In a right vagus nerve lesion, to which side does the uvula deviate on saying 'ah'?
questions.explain: The palatal muscles on the lesion side are weak, so the uvula is pulled toward the normal (left) side.

open.q: In a right vagus nerve lesion, to which side does the uvula deviate on saying 'ah'?

questions.q: Which muscles are supplied by the spinal accessory nerve?
questions.explain: The spinal root of CN XI supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. Injury in the posterior triangle causes a drooping shoulder.

open.q: Which two muscles are supplied by the spinal accessory nerve?

questions.q: When a patient protrudes the tongue it deviates to the left. Which nerve is damaged?
questions.explain: The genioglossus on the damaged side cannot push the tongue forward, so the intact right genioglossus pushes the tongue toward the weak left side.

open.q: When a patient protrudes the tongue it deviates to the left. Which nerve is damaged?

questions.q: A lesion selectively damages the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus in the medulla. Which function is most directly affected?
options: Parasympathetic preganglionic output to thoracic and abdominal viscera
Somatic motor supply to the muscles of the tongue
Branchial motor supply to the muscles of facial expression
Sympathetic supply to the upper limb
questions.explain: The dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus contains preganglionic parasympathetic neurons that project through the vagus nerve to thoracic and abdominal viscera. The hypoglossal nucleus supplies tongue muscles, while facial expression muscles receive branchial motor fibres from the facial motor nucleus.
